{"id": "53:37/q05", "question": "How many scrolls or books were attributed to Abraham?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q05/p1", "position": "Abraham received ten scrolls.", "reasons": "Abū Dharr's report through Ibn al-Jawzī also gives Moses ten before the Torah. {"id": "53:37/q06", "question": "What counsel is reported from Abraham's scrolls?", "turns_on": "The reports preserve different admonitions from the scrolls.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q06/p1", "position": "A king should answer the oppressed person's prayer instead of amassing wealth.", "reasons": "Bursevī's scroll report includes even an oppressed unbeliever."}, {"id": "53:37/q06/p2", "position": "A wise person should allot time to prayer, reflection, self-accounting and lawful needs, and guard the tongue.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports that speech counts among one's deeds and one should know one's era."}]}
{"id": "53:37/q07", "question": "Why are Abraham and Moses singled out?", "turns_on": "Whether the selection highlights the historical rule against transferred guilt or addresses communities claiming prophetic ancestry.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q07/p1", "position": "Abraham first opposed holding people responsible for relatives' crimes, and Moses confirmed or continued the rule.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı place the earlier custom between Noah and Abraham or before Abraham and say his law ended it through Moses."}, {"id": "53:37/q07/p2", "position": "Their teachings correct those who claim descent from them grants salvation.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says Quraysh claimed Abraham as ancestor and leader, while the People of the Book claimed both prophets; their teaching and sacrifices, rather than descent, determine the point."}]}
{"id": "53:37/q08", "question": "How is وَفَّىٰ read?", "turns_on": "Doubling or lightening the fāʾ, with some commentators assigning distinct emphases.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q08/p1", "position": "The common or majority reading doubles the fāʾ: waffā.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn identify it as common or majority; Zamakhsharī and Qurṭubī say doubling intensifies or indicates complete fulfillment."}, {"id": "53:37/q08/p2", "position": "It is also read with a light, undoubled fāʾ: wafā.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is repeatedly named; other transmitters include Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, Abū Mālik, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, Abū Umāma, Zayd ibn ʿAlī and a report from the Prophet. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says interpretation remains the same; Qurṭubī glosses truthfulness in word and deed, Jishumī keeping promise and covenant, and Qāshānī the primordial covenant."}]}
{"id": "53:37/q09", "question": "What does وَفَّىٰ mean and imply?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbal force is full completion, covenant fidelity, or emphatic expression of unusually severe trials.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q09/p1", "position": "It means to fulfill or complete fully, reaching the end of what is due.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says attaining the intended end; Thaʿlabī and Wāḥidī liken tawfiya to full payment of a right or wages, citing 3:57 and 35:30; Jishumī distinguishes giving in full from meeting one's due. Naḥḥās, Qurṭubī, Nasafī, Bursevī and al-Samīn stress completion or breadth, and 2:124 supplies a parallel."}, {"id": "53:37/q09/p2", "position": "It emphasizes faithful keeping of a covenant or promise.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers covenant-fulfillment as the apparent sense and connects it to the confirmed dream in 37:105–106; Bayḍāwī says Abraham went to great lengths for his covenant. {"id": "53:37/q10", "question": "What did Abraham fulfill?", "turns_on": "Whether the unrestricted omitted object embraces all obedience or identifies a specific command, test, covenant, ritual, scripture passage or devotional practice; reports supply different particulars and some chains are questioned.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q10/p1", "position": "He fulfilled every divine command, duty, trial and act of obedience.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says everything imposed on him; Abū al-ʿĀliya and others connect this to 2:124. Ibn Kathīr adds 16:123, exemplary obedience and release from Fire; examples include circumcision, pilgrimage, fire, sacrifice, migration, hospitality and servitude. Some notes join conveying with obedience, explaining the law, or enduring the mission."}, {"id": "53:37/q10/p3", "position": "He conveyed the rule that no soul bears another's burden and ended earlier transferred liability.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports that kin, allies, spouses, masters or neighbors had been punished for others; ʿAmr ibn Aws and Hudhayl place the practice before Abraham, with Hudhayl tracing it to Noah. Reports say no one else fully practiced them, or that fulfilling one portion counts as fulfilling that share."}, {"id": "53:37/q10/p7", "position": "He prayed four early-day rakʿahs as his daily duty.", "reasons": "The reports often identify the practice as ḍuḥā. A sacred hadith promises sufficiency for the day's remainder to one who prays four units; Ṭabarī voices chain concerns about the prophetic reports, Ibn Kathīr names Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr as weakening this chain, and al-Suyūṭī and Ālūsī call it weak."}, {"id": "53:37/q10/p8", "position": "He recited the morning and evening glorification of 30:17–18 regularly.", "reasons": "Reports explain that God named him His intimate friend who fulfilled because of the recitation. {"id": "53:37/q11", "question": "How is Abraham's fulfillment related grammatically to the following no-bearer statement?", "turns_on": "Whether the next clause functions as the object of fulfillment or as independent scroll content, and whether it is understood as fronted.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q11/p1", "position": "On the message-delivery reading, the following 'that' clause is governed by 'fulfilled'.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says the particle an is accusative under waffā in the first interpretation."}, {"id": "53:37/q11/p2", "position": "The no-bearer statement is content of Moses' and Abraham's scrolls, not a restriction on what Abraham fulfilled.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī gives this analysis and rejects limiting the general verb to that one teaching; Ibn ʿAbbās says the rule through the rest is in Moses' scrolls."}, {"id": "53:37/q11/p3", "position": "The no-bearer clause is fronted in meaning and belongs with the mention of both sets of scrolls.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī reports this in conjunction with the son-sacrifice interpretation."}]}
{"id": "53:37/q12", "question": "Why is Abraham described as one who fulfilled?", "turns_on": "Whether the epithet chiefly explains his exceptional merit, its universal recognition, or its rebuke to descendants.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q12/p1", "position": "His extraordinary trials warrant the epithet.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the sacrifice alone suffices; Bursevī lists fire, sacrifice, migration, leaving family in a barren valley and guest-seeking; Bayḍāwī adds refusing Gabriel's help."}, {"id": "53:37/q12/p2", "position": "All major audiences accepted this praise of Abraham.", "reasons": "Rāzī says Jews, polytheists and Muslims agreed on Abraham's fidelity, whereas polytheists might hesitate to praise Moses."}, {"id": "53:37/q12/p3", "position": "His faithfulness exposes descendants who claim his favor while abandoning his teaching.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr indicts Arabs' idolatry despite Abraham's transmission; Islāḥī contrasts Abraham's standing through obedience with descendants' reliance on ancestry."}]}
{"id": "53:37/q13", "question": "What inward fulfillment is attributed to Abraham?", "turns_on": "The inward accounts locate fulfillment in surrender, witnessing, or spiritual unity and service.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q13/p1", "position": "He left the self behind, bearing every trial as a blessing in God's presence.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports the unnamed saying."}, {"id": "53:37/q13/p2", "position": "He fulfilled by sincere, faithful witnessing in every condition and deed.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports Jaʿfar's definition."}, {"id": "53:37/q13/p3", "position": "He surrendered self, heart, son and wealth to God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ gives four offerings: self to fire, heart to the Merciful, son to sacrifice, wealth to brothers; Abū al-Qāsim recalls ransom of the son at 37:107."}, {"id": "53:37/q13/p4", "position": "He surrendered existence in annihilating unity, then served and conveyed in steadfast subsistence.", "reasons": "Qāshānī also allows completion of the divine testing words and, with the light reading, fidelity to the primordial covenant until attaining unity, citing 6:79."}]}
{"id": "53:37/q14", "question": "How does the verse and its scroll citation connect to its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Which prior argument and audience the earlier-scriptures citation principally addresses.", "positions": [{"id": "53:37/q14/p1", "position": "The scrolls restate individual recompense already raised in 53:30–31.", "reasons": "Rāzī links both passages through recompense; Asad says the prophets conveyed lasting ethical truths, with 2:124 as a parallel."}, {"id": "53:37/q14/p2", "position": "The citation challenges a person who gave briefly then withheld, possibly a scriptured person.", "reasons": "Rāzī proposes the turn from idolaters to a book-holder at 53:33 and says his scrolls already taught individual responsibility; the bodily-rights contrast is to 53:34."}, {"id": "53:37/q14/p3", "position": "The earlier scriptures counter polytheist claims of angelic intercession and set out creation, duties and recompense.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī links them to rejection of idols as God's daughters, creation and governance, resurrection, destruction of Noah's, ʿĀd's, Thamūd's and the overturned cities' peoples; the sūra then warns of the Hour and commands prostration. Study Quran calls these enduring truths after creation and transitions."}, {"id": "53:37/q14/p4", "position": "The citation redirects Abraham's and Moses' claimed descendants toward those prophets' teachings and sacrifices.", "reasons": "Islāḥī identifies Quraysh as primary and People of the Book as secondary addressees, and rejects an assumption of Paradise based on descent."}]}

{"id": "53:38/q01", "question": "How is أَلَّا تَزِرُ parsed and attached to the preceding report of the scrolls?", "turns_on": "The grammatical force of أن and whether the clause substitutes for earlier material, supplies an omitted predicate, takes an implied verb, or explains the written report.", "positions": [{"id": "53:38/q01/p1", "position": "أن is lightened from أنَّ, with an implicit subject, and its clause is genitive as an apposition to ما or the reported contents of the scrolls.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Tabrisī, Rāzī, and Samīn identify the preceding ما as the appositional base; Tabrisī calls it relative. Samīn expressly prefers the genitive case. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it specification of the scriptures' general contents."}, {"id": "53:38/q01/p2", "position": "The clause is nominative, supplying the predicate of an omitted هو or ذلك or independently clarifying what the scrolls contain.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Wahidi phrase it as an answer to 'What is in the scrolls?' Samīn gives an omitted هو or ذلك. Naḥḥās allows a new nominative clause. The lightened أن and implicit matter-pronoun remain possible in this parse, according to the sources that give both analyses."}, {"id": "53:38/q01/p3", "position": "The clause is accusative, either appositional to ما or governed by an omitted أعني.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās gives the accusative apposition; Samīn permits omitted أعني and notes that the verb is omitted with this sort of implicit subject."}, {"id": "53:38/q01/p4", "position": "أن is explanatory, introducing an explanation of the meaningful speech conveyed by the written scriptures.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says written material can convey speech in meaning, allowing explanatory أن."}]}

{"id": "53:38/q07", "question": "What earlier practice did Abraham's teaching end?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in whom they say was liable for whose wrong and whether the wrong was specifically a killing; some give only the general practice.", "positions": [{"id": "53:38/q07/p1", "position": "People had been held for someone else's sin until Abraham conveyed the rule.", "reasons": "ʿAmr ibn Aws reports the earlier practice generally. {"id": "53:38/q08", "question": "How did Abraham fulfill his duty in relation to this teaching?", "turns_on": "Which act is taken as Abraham's fulfillment: conveying this rule, action after his dream about his son, or seeking forgiveness for his father.", "positions": [{"id": "53:38/q08/p1", "position": "He fulfilled his task by conveying or establishing the rule that none bears another's burden.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid in Jishumī, Mujāhid and ʿIkrima in Durr, Abū al-ʿĀliya, and Ibn ʿAbbās in Qurtubī make delivery of the rule the fulfillment.
